We estimate that approximately 200,000 tons of tailings storage capacity remains available under our current permits; additional capacity beyond that, through the next phase of the dry-stack tailings facility (Phase 3), will require permit amendments and related construction.

At milling rates for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, we project that we would exhaust that capacity in the second quarter of 2028, before Phase 3 is expected to be permitted and constructed.

In an effort to maintain operational continuity and to extend the remaining capacity until Phase 3 is in place, we plan to suppress throughput as described below under “Strategic Focus and Path to 440 Tons Per Day.” Even at the reduced rate, however, we expect to exhaust our tailings storage capacity unless Phase 3 is permitted and constructed during the 2029 construction season.
To sustain operations at or near this permitted rate, we will need to amend our quartz mining license (“QML”) and water license (“WL”) to address these constraints.

The process for securing these amendments includes submission of a Project Proposal to the Yukon Environmental and Socio‑economic Assessment Board (“YESAB”), which we currently intend to submit by year-end 2026.
FNNND previously entered into a Comprehensive Cooperation and Benefits Agreement ("CBA") for Keno Hill, and we believe they remain supportive of the project.

We currently estimate that this overall process could be completed by approximately mid‑2029, although each sequential step in this process is subject to its own timing variability, and delays at any stage would affect the overall timeline.

At current mining rates, we project that the waste rock production limit could be reached by approximately mid‑2027, at which point waste rock production would need to be halted absent receipt of a QML amendment.

The planned suppression in throughput described below under “Strategic Focus and Path to 440 Tons Per Day” is intended to keep waste rock production and storage within our existing QML limits until the amended QML is received, which we currently expect by approximately mid‑2029.

If suppressing production is not effective in preserving waste rock disposal capacity, or if neither the QML amendment nor the separate changes to our QML that we are seeking (independent of the QML amendment process described above) is received in 2029, we expect to exhaust our waste rock storage capacity, even at the reduced rate, and mine production could be further curtailed or stop until the amended permits…

Our near‑term strategic focus is to advance permitting and execute key infrastructure projects to place the mine on a path toward achieving sustainable production at its currently permitted rate of 440 tons per day.
At that rate and at current prices, we expect Keno Hill would generate sustained positive free cash flow while preserving optionality for potential expansion beyond 440 tons per day.
As discussed above, to sustain operations at or near this permitted rate, we will need to amend our QML and WL to expand our tailings, waste rock and water treatment capacity.

We expect to begin suppressing throughput in the fourth quarter of 2026 to approximately 300 tons per day, with further suppression, expected beginning in January 2027 to levels significantly below third quarter 2026 throughput.
We expect to provide 2027 production guidance for Keno Hill in February 2027.

Available capacity for water treatment, tailings storage, and waste rock disposal under our current permits will not support our current levels of production until our QML and WL are amended and the related projects constructed.

We are currently targeting license amendments to be finalized by mid-2029, after which, once the related infrastructure is constructed, we would expect to ramp back up toward throughput of 440 tons per day.

If those permits or the related infrastructure projects are delayed beyond our current schedule, throughput could be constrained further or interrupted entirely until the necessary tailings and waste rock storage capacity is in place.
We expect silver production to decline by proportionally less than throughput because, during this period, we expect to be more selective in both mining and processing.

In the mill, we expect to preferentially process higher-grade material and stockpile lower-grade material for later processing.

Each reporting period we assess our deferred tax balances based on a review of long-range forecasts and quarterly activity.
We analyze our deferred tax assets and, if it is determined that we will not realize all or a portion of our deferred tax assets, we record or increase a valuation allowance.

Conversely, if it is determined we will ultimately more likely than not be able to realize all or a portion of the related benefits for which a valuation allowance has been provided, all or a portion of the related valuation allowance will be reduced.

Consistent with that strategy, we aim to maintain an acceptable level of debt and sufficient liquidity to fund debt service costs, operations, capital expenditures, exploration and pre-development projects, while returning cash to stockholders through dividends and potential share repurchases.

At September 30, 2026, we had $691.6 million in cash and cash equivalents, of which $9.6 million was held in foreign subsidiaries local currency that we anticipate utilizing for near-term operating, exploration or capital costs by those foreign subsidiaries.
